sights.w: One of the Ryūkyū Hassha, the eight shrines given royal patronage by the Ryūkyū Kingdom, near Shikinaen in Hantagawa. Its origin story centres on a sacred cave, which the shrine opens to visitors on the 1st and 15th of each month.
sights.k: Royal-patronage shrine of the Ryūkyū Eight, with a sacred cave

sights.w: One of the Ryūkyū Hassha, dedicated to Kumano Gongen and long prayed to for safe voyages by tribute ships. Founded beside Naha harbour (per the 1713 Ryūkyū-koku Yuraiki), designated a National Treasure in 1935, destroyed in 1945, re-established in 1961 and moved to Onoyama Park in 1975.
sights.k: Ryūkyū's harbour shrine for safe voyages, rebuilt in Onoyama Park

sights.w: One of the Ryūkyū Hassha, founded in the Tianshun era (1457–64) and enshrining Emperor Ōjin, Empress Jingū and Tamayori-hime; the only Hachiman shrine among the eight. A short walk from Asato and Omoromachi stations.
One of the Ryūkyū Hassha, founded in the Chenghua era (1465–87) and enshrining Izanami with Hayatamao and Kotosakao (the Kumano deities); annual festival on 15 May. Tucked into a hillside in Tomari.
sights.k: Hillside Kumano shrine of the Ryūkyū Eight in Tomari

sights.n: Gajanbira Park night view (がじゃんびら公園)
sights.w: Hilltop park on the Oroku heights, the night-view spot closest to Naha Airport: a 500 m promenade looks across Naha port to the city lights. The name comes from Okinawan dialect, gajan (mosquito) + bira (slope).
